question.problem: Let $f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(z).$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,1,\pi ).$
question.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,1,\pi )$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,1,\pi )+∇f(0,1,\pi )\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(0,1,\pi )=-1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =y{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(0,1,\pi )=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(0,1,\pi )=0, \\ {f}_{z} & =-{e}^{xy}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(0,1,\pi )=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(0,1,\pi )$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(0,1,\pi ) & =⟨{f}_{x}(0,1,\pi ),{f}_{y}(0,1,\pi ),{f}_{z}(0,1,\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,1,\pi )+∇f(0,1,\pi )\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\pi ⟩ \\  & ≈-1+⟨-1,0,0⟩\cdot ⟨x,y-1,z-\pi ⟩ \\  & ≈-1-x.\end{aligned}
$$
